title: The Investor-Ready Story Audit
subtitle: Score whether your narrative is clear, credible, and specific enough to raise capital and win clients before you spend a dollar amplifying it.

questions.text: Open your homepage or pitch deck right now. Count the adjectives in the first paragraph: 'leading,' 'innovative,' 'best-in-class.' How many are there?

answers.label: Five or more. My opening is mostly description and positioning language.
Three or four. I know they're there but haven't replaced them with numbers yet.
One or two. I've tried to keep the language tight.
Zero. Every claim in that paragraph points to a specific number I own.

questions.text: What does your single most credibility-building sentence look like right now?

answers.label: Something like 'we're disrupting the X market' or 'the leading platform for Y.'
A general traction claim: 'strong growth' or 'thousands of customers.'
A real number, but one I probably share with other companies in the space.
A specific stat that no one else in my category can claim verbatim.
A specific stat with a time window: before, after, and how long it took.

questions.text: If an investor asked you to pull the source for your most important claim in thirty seconds, could you?

answers.label: Probably not. The claim is more directional than documented.
Eventually, but I'd need to dig for it.
Yes, but it's an estimate rather than a hard number.
Yes. I know exactly where the data lives and can pull it in under a minute.

low.headline: Your proof layer is leaking on first read.
low.text: Words like 'leading,' 'innovative,' and 'best-in-class' cost nothing to write, so they prove nothing. Your first paragraph is where the reader decides whether you've earned two more minutes. Right now, you probably haven't.
steps: Pull up your homepage and your one-pager. Highlight every adjective in the first three sentences.
For each one, ask: is there a specific number I own that makes this point better? If yes, swap it. If no, cut the adjective and restructure the sentence.
Find the three numbers in your business that nobody else in your category can claim. Those are the sentences that should open your pitch.

mid.headline: You have real proof. You're not leading with it.
mid.text: The numbers are there. They're just buried. Investors and clients make the call in the first thirty seconds, and if your best proof is in slide nine or paragraph four, most people never see it. The fix isn't inventing better numbers. It's putting the ones you have in front.
steps: Audit your opening: what's the first specific, checkable claim a reader sees? If it's not in the first two sentences, move it.
Test whether your claims are uniquely yours. Could a competitor write the same sentence about their company? If yes, that claim isn't doing the job. The words need to belong to you specifically.
Add a time window to your best number. '$X in revenue' is weaker than '$X in revenue in the first 90 days.' Specificity is credibility.

high.headline: Your proof layer is solid. Protect it as you scale.
high.text: You've done the hard part. You've replaced adjectives with claims that are uniquely yours and checkable. The risk at this stage is drift. As the team grows and copy gets edited by more hands, the vague language creeps back in. Keep the standard.
steps: Document your three core proof points in a single internal reference so everyone writing about the company uses the same specific numbers.
Before any major pitch or publishing push, run a quick audit: count the adjectives in the first paragraph. If the number goes up, fix it before it goes out.
Find one more number you own that isn't in the story yet. There's usually one sitting in your data that's more striking than what you're currently leading with.

questions.text: Think about the last ten pieces of content you published. Which metric is actually running your content decisions?

answers.label: Views, impressions, or follower growth. Those are the numbers I check first.
Engagement: likes, comments, shares. I treat those as signals that content is working.
A mix. I look at both reach and business outcomes, but reach is faster to see.
Calls booked, replies from target accounts, or deal movement. Engagement is nice but it's not what I optimize for.

questions.text: Can you name a specific piece of content from the last three months that directly contributed to a client conversation or a warm investor intro?

answers.label: No. I can't connect any specific content to a specific business outcome.
Maybe one, but I'm not sure if the content caused it or if the timing was coincidence.
Yes, one or two. I know which posts are doing real work.
Yes. I track this and I know which formats and topics drive calls.

questions.text: What does your highest-performing content look like when you measure by business outcome rather than by reach?

answers.label: I've never run that comparison. I measure by reach.
I've thought about it but I don't have clean enough data to answer it.
I have a rough sense. It tends to be the more personal or specific posts, not the broad ones.
I know exactly which format and topic drove the most real business, and it wasn't my most-viewed post.

low.headline: You're running the wrong scoreboard.
low.text: Two hundred thousand impressions can book zero calls. Eleven hundred impressions can book three discovery calls and close a client. Those aren't hypothetical numbers. Attention feels like progress because it's visible and immediate. Revenue attribution is slower and harder to see, so it loses the argument every time someone looks at a dashboard. The metric that makes you feel like you're winning and the metric that actually grows the business rarely come from the same posts.
steps: Pull your last ten posts. Next to each one, write the actual business outcome, not the impressions. Calls booked, replies from target accounts, investor intros, anything concrete.
Find the post with the fewest impressions that drove the most real business. That post tells you more about your story than everything else combined.
For the next month, before publishing anything, ask one question: if this gets exactly the reach my average post gets, does it still book a call?

mid.headline: You're starting to track the right things. Keep going.
mid.text: You know the revenue signal exists. You've seen it work a couple of times. The gap right now is consistency. You haven't yet built the feedback loop tight enough to know which specific variables drive business outcomes versus reach. That's the next thing to solve.
steps: Set up a simple log. A spreadsheet is fine. Track every piece of content you publish with the business outcome in the same row, not two tabs over.
After thirty posts, look for the pattern. Is it the topic? The format? The opening line? The answer is usually more specific than 'personal posts do better.'
Test the posts you almost didn't publish. Those are often the ones that land, because the hesitation usually means it's specific enough to feel exposed. Specific is what books calls.

high.headline: You've found the revenue signal. Now scale from it.
high.text: You know which content moves the business and which just moves numbers. That's a real advantage. The next question is whether you can reverse-engineer the pattern and apply it consistently, or whether it still feels like luck when it works.
steps: Document the three variables your highest-revenue-signal content shares. Is it the opening line format? A specific topic cluster? The level of personal specificity? Name the pattern explicitly.
Build a simple brief template from those variables and use it before writing anything new.
The posts you're holding back because they feel too specific or too honest: publish them. That discomfort is usually the signal that it's worth running.

questions.text: Where does the majority of your content effort go each week?

answers.label: Company page. That's where we keep things consistent and on-brand.
Roughly split. I try to post to both the brand page and my personal profile.
Mostly personal profile, but I repurpose to the brand page too.
Personal profile. The company page is secondary and I'm at peace with that.

questions.text: When you post in your own name, how often do you include a real point of view: a specific opinion, a number from your own experience, or something you got wrong?

answers.label: Rarely. My posts share information or updates rather than a take.
Sometimes, but I usually soften the opinion by the time I publish.
Often. I have a take in most posts, even if I hedge it slightly.
Almost always. My posts start from a specific belief or a number from my own work.
Always. Every post I publish has a claim I can defend with a number or a story I was in.

questions.text: When you send a cold pitch or investor email, what percentage of recipients already know your name or your work before they open it?

answers.label: Under 5%. Almost everyone I reach out to has never heard of me.
10 to 20%. A few recognize the name but most don't.
30 to 50%. A real chunk of the list already knows who I am.
Over half. The cold email isn't really cold anymore for most of my targets.

low.headline: You're building trust for a logo when you should be building it for yourself.
low.text: Personal profiles consistently outperform brand pages for founders. Worse design, no ad budget, just a real person with a real point of view. LinkedIn's own 2026 data puts company page reach at around 5% of the feed, and that number is still falling. Every hour you put into the brand page instead of your own profile is a compounding mistake. You are the distribution. The brand page is what you send people to after they already trust you.
steps: For the next thirty days, publish nothing to the company page that you haven't already published from your personal profile.
Write your next three posts in first person with a specific number or lesson from your own experience. Your face, your name, your take.

Map everyone in your next investor outreach or sales push who already follows you personally. That number is your baseline warm room. It's probably smaller than you want. The goal is to grow it before the ask, not after.

mid.headline: You're in the right place. The gap is consistency and specificity.
mid.text: You know your personal profile should be the priority, and you're mostly there. The thing that separates this tier from the next one isn't effort. It's the willingness to put a real opinion on the line instead of sharing information. Information posts build traffic. Opinion posts build the warm room.
steps: Run a quick audit of your last ten personal posts. How many include a specific claim you'd defend in a room? How many are updates or information you're passing along? The ratio tells you exactly where you're hedging.
Pick one belief you hold about your category that most people in your space would push back on. Write that post next. If you've been drafting it for two weeks and not publishing, publish it.
Set a target: 50% warm opens on your next outreach round. Work backward to figure how many people need to follow your personal profile before you send the ask.

high.headline: Your distribution is working. Now protect the room.
high.text: The warm room you've built is an asset that's hard to manufacture quickly. An investor who already knows your work reads your cold email differently than one who's never heard of you. You've put in the work. The question now is whether you're converting that attention into the right asks at the right moment.
steps: Audit your publishing cadence. What's the gap between your last post and your last pitch or outreach push? If you went quiet before asking, you're withdrawing from an account you didn't restock first.
Map the overlap between your existing audience and your active pipeline. How warm is the room actually? Adjust your outreach sequence based on who already knows you.
The founders who built this audience before they needed it got here by publishing before the ask. Keep that standard even when the round is going well.

questions.text: An investor asks: 'Why is your category inevitable right now? Not why your company is good. Why does this problem get solved in the next three years regardless of whether you exist?' How ready are you?

answers.label: I'd mostly talk about our product and team. I haven't built the 'why now' argument separately.
I have a rough version, but I'm not sure it's different from what everyone else in my space says.
I have a specific 'why now' I can say in three sentences with a market data point.
It's the foundation of my pitch. I explain the category timing before I explain the company.

questions.text: How does your story handle the AI moment: directly and specifically, or by avoidance?

answers.label: I don't address it. It feels tangential to what we're building.
I mention AI in the deck because I think I need to, but the connection to our product is thin.
AI genuinely touches our product and I lead with that, but I could be more specific about how.
I address it directly: AI is core to how we work, or I explain in one sentence why our category doesn't need the pivot.

questions.text: Can you say in one sentence what makes your growth number different from every other growth number an investor heard this week?

answers.label: Not really. I lead with the growth number but I don't have a sentence that contextualizes it.
I have context: market size, competitive positioning. But it takes several sentences.
I have a specific comparison point that makes the number land harder than the raw figure.
One sentence, no jargon, that makes the number feel inevitable rather than just impressive.

questions.text: Have you stress-tested the weakest part of your story with someone whose job in that conversation was to find the holes?

answers.label: No. I haven't put it in front of anyone who was actively trying to break it.
I know where it's weak but I've been avoiding that question in pitch conversations.
I've gotten the hard question and I have an answer, but I'm not confident in it.
Yes. I know the weak point, I've addressed it directly in the deck, and I can handle the pushback.

low.headline: Your story stops at the company. It needs to start with the category.
low.text: Growing 3x doesn't close rounds on its own anymore. Every founder in a live deal has a growth number. The ones getting checks can explain why their category is inevitable right now, separate from the fact that their business is working. If you can't say in under sixty seconds why this problem gets solved in the next three years regardless of whether you exist, an investor who's seen thirty pitches this week already knows how the meeting ends.
steps: Write one paragraph, just for yourself and not for the deck, that explains why this category is happening now. What changed in the past eighteen months that makes this problem urgent? What would have to be true in 2028 for your category to have failed?
Find one specific data point that a skeptical investor couldn't argue with. Pull it from market research, not from your own numbers. That data point proves the timing.

If AI genuinely connects to your product, lead with the connection specifically. If it doesn't, explain why your category doesn't need the pivot in one sentence and move on. Answer that question before it gets asked.

mid.headline: You have a category story. It needs to be faster and more specific.
mid.text: The 'why now' is in there. It just takes too many sentences to land. Investors make the category call in the first two minutes, and if you're spending those minutes on product features or team background, you're letting them fill in the category logic themselves. They'll fill it in wrong half the time, and you won't know it happened.
steps: Cut your current 'why now' down to three sentences: the shift that happened, the window that opened, and why that window closes. Time yourself. If it takes more than forty-five seconds, cut again.
Test the AI question directly. Ask a founder in a different category to push back on your AI story as hard as they can. If you're defensive, the investors will be too.

Find the one weakness in your story that a skeptical investor would find fastest. Write a direct answer to it and put it in the deck before they ask. Addressing the hard thing proactively reads as confidence.

high.headline: Your category story is solid. Make sure it travels without you.
high.text: You can tell the story in the room. The question is whether it holds when you're not there: when an investor is describing your company to a partner, or when a client is explaining why they picked you to their board. If the story only works when you're telling it, it's not done yet.
steps: Ask the last investor or client who said yes to your pitch to describe your company back to you in their own words. Listen for what they kept and what they dropped. What they kept is what's actually landing.

Write a two-sentence version of the category story, tight enough that someone else could repeat it after one conversation. If you can't get it to two sentences without losing the core, it's not specific enough yet.
Give your deck to someone who's never heard your pitch and ask them to find the weakest point. If they find something you already knew about and haven't addressed, that's the next thing to fix.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: In 30 minutes I'll show you which two gaps to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing.

persona_selector.text: Where does a weak story cost you the most right now?

answers.label: In the fundraising process: getting meetings but not checks
In sales: prospects don't convert the way my numbers say they should
In content: posting consistently but not booking calls
All three. I think the same gap is showing up everywhere
